title: Prevalence of nonalcoholic steatohepatitis in Japanese patients with morbid obesity undergoing bariatric surgery.
text_summary: 本文围绕“Prevalence of nonalcoholic steatohepatitis in Japanese patients with morbid obesity undergoing bariatric surgery.”开展研究，具体研究方法、结果和结论见论文正文。

ORIGINAL ARTICLE—LIVER, PANCREAS, AND BILIARY TRACT
Prevalence of nonalcoholic steatohepatitis in Japanese patients
with morbid obesity undergoing bariatric surgery
Yosuke Seki1 • Satoru Kakizaki2 • Norio Horiguchi2 • Hiroaki Hashizume2 •
Hiroki Tojima2 • Yuichi Yamazaki2 • Ken Sato2 • Motoyasu Kusano2 •
Masanobu Yamada2 • Kazunori Kasama1
Received: 26 May 2015 / Accepted: 3 August 2015
 Springer Japan 2015
Abstract
Background
Patients with morbid obesity selected for
bariatric surgery have a high prevalence of nonalcoholic
steatohepatitis (NASH); however, the incidence is varied
and depends on race. The prevalence of NASH in obese
Japanese patients is unknown. We evaluated the prevalence
of NASH in a prospective cohort of Japanese patients with
morbid obesity.
Methods
From October 2009 to July 2011, consecutive
patients requiring bariatric surgery underwent a liver
biopsy during the operation. The indications for bariatric
surgery followed the guidelines of the Asia–Paciﬁc Meta-
bolic and Bariatric Surgery Society.
Results
One hundred two patients (55 males and 47
females, age 42.7 ± 10.7 years) were analyzed. The mean
body mass index was 42.1 ± 8.2 kg/m2. Among the 102
patients, 84 patients (82.4 %) had nonalcoholic fatty liver
disease and 79 patients (77.5 %) had NASH. The grading
and staging of NASH by Brunt’s classiﬁcation were as
follows: grade 0 steatosis, one patient; grade 1 steatosis, 35
patients; grade 2 steatosis, 32 patients; grade 3 steatosis, 11
patients; stage 1 ﬁbrosis, 25 patients; stage 2 ﬁbrosis, 38
patients; stage 3 ﬁbrosis, 16 patients, stage 4 ﬁbrosis, no
patients. The body weight, waist–hip ratio, visceral fat
area, and aspartate aminotransferase, alanine aminotrans-
ferase, c-glutamyl transpeptidase, fasting plasma glucose,
fasting plasma insulin, C peptide, hemoglobin A1c, and
homeostasis model assessment insulin resistance levels
were signiﬁcantly elevated in the NASH group in com-
parison with the non-NASH group. The platelet count was
signiﬁcantly decreased in the NASH group. The waist–hip
ratio and the alanine aminotransferase, fasting plasma
glucose, and homeostasis model assessment insulin resis-
tance levels were found to be independent predictors of
NASH in a multivariate analysis.
Conclusion
The prevalence of NASH was 77.5 % in this
prospective Japanese cohort. The prevalence of NASH in
Japanese morbidly obese patients was extremely high, and
early intervention should be undertaken.

Nonalcoholic steatohepatitis  Morbidly
obesity  Bariatric surgery

Introduction
The number of obese patients is increasing worldwide, and
the increase in the number of patients with morbid obesity
is a major social problem [1]. Morbid obesity tends to be

complicated with metabolic diseases such as type II dia-
betes mellitus, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and ischemic
heart disease. The incidence of nonalcoholic fatty liver
disease (NAFLD) is also increasing in patients with morbid
obesity, and it is now considered to be the commonest liver
disease in the USA [2, 3]. Although the prevalence of
NAFLD in the general population is estimated to range
from 3 to 24 %, depending on the deﬁnition [4, 5], morbid
obesity is associated with a much higher prevalence of
NAFLD and nonalcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH) [6–24].
Machado et al. [25] reviewed the prevalence of NAFLD
and NASH in morbidly obese patients undergoing bariatric
surgery from 12 studies with a total of 1620 patients. The
prevalence of NAFLD was 91 % (range 85–98 %) and that
of NASH was 37 % (range 24–98 %), with unexpected
cirrhosis in 1.7 % of patients (range 1–7 %).
Although the prevalence of morbid obesity is low in Japan
(0.25–0.3 %) in comparison with the USA [26, 27], it is
increasing. We previously investigated the clinical charac-
teristics of severely obese Japanese patients undergoing
laparoscopic Roux-en-Y gastric bypass surgery [28]. In our
previous retrospective study, the prevalence of NAFLD in
morbidly obese Japanese patients was 76.3 % (45 of 59
patients) [28]. Because a liver biopsy is needed to diagnose
NASH, we could not calculate the exact prevalence of NASH
in morbidly obese Japanese patients in the previous study
[28]. The prevalence of NASH in morbidly obese patients
selected for bariatric surgery has been investigated in other
countries, and ranged from 2.6 % [19] to 98 % [9]. However,
there have been no previous reports regarding the prevalence
of NASH in morbidly obese patients in Japan.
Because a liver biopsy is invasive for patients, knowing the
predictive factors for NASH can be helpful for patients.
Insulin resistance [6], hypertension [6], diabetes mellitus [12–
14], age [8, 18], and abnormal liver function test results [6, 13]
have all been identiﬁed as predictive factors for existing
NASH. A combination of two or three of these factors has
been demonstrated to increase the risk of NASH [6, 18].
However, there have been no studies to identify the predictive
factors for NASH in morbidly obese Japanese patients.
The aims of the present study were to determine the
prevalence of NASH and to identify the clinical and/or
biochemical factors predicting the presence of NASH in a
prospective cohort of morbidly obese Japanese patients
selected for bariatric surgery at a single center.
Patients and methods
Study design
This prospective study involved consecutive obese patients
undergoing bariatric surgery for the management of morbid
obesity at a single center (Weight Loss and Metabolic
Surgery Center, Yotsuya Medical Cube, Tokyo, Japan),
and all were enrolled from October 2009 until July 2011.
The main purpose of this study is to evaluate the preva-
lence of NASH in Japanese patients with morbid obesity.
The secondary purpose is to identify the factors that are
predictive of NASH in morbidly obese Japanese patients.
In accordance with previous reports [6, 10], the study
sample size was set at 100 to study the key variables. The
exclusion criteria included a reported history of daily
consumption of alcohol of more than 20 g/day, a clinical
diagnosis of a liver disease of another cause (including
viral hepatitis, autoimmune hepatitis, primary biliary cir-
rhosis, drug-induced liver disease, hemochromatosis, bil-
iary
obstruction,
and
Wilson’s
disease),
and
severe
complications, such as congestive heart failure. Patients
who underwent a second bariatric surgical procedure were
also excluded. All patients provided written informed
consent for participation. As the indications for bariatric
surgery, we followed the criteria established in 2005 by the
Asia–Paciﬁc Bariatric Surgery Group consensus meeting
[29] as follows; Asian patients with a body mass index
(BMI) greater than 37 kg/m2 or greater than 32 kg/m2 with
diabetes or two other obesity-related comorbidities, and
failure to show any improvement with nonsurgical treat-
ment. Patients underwent a Roux-en-Y gastric bypass or
sleeve gastrectomy, which was performed laparoscopically.
The standard clinical, anthropometric (weight, height,
and waist and hip circumferences), and biochemical mea-
surements, including aspartate aminotransferase, alanine
aminotransferase (ALT), c-glutamyl transpeptidase, fasting
blood
insulin,
fasting
plasma
glucose,
C peptide,
hemoglobin A1c, and cholesterol levels, were obtained
before the bariatric surgery. All blood samples were col-
lected after patients had fasted overnight. The homeostasis
model assessment insulin resistance (HOMA-IR) index
was used as an index of insulin resistance and was calcu-
lated by the following formula: glucose concentration (mg/
dL) 9 insulin
concentration
(lU/mL)/405.
Computed
tomography was performed, and subcutaneous and visceral
fat areas were calculated. The body fat percentage and
basal metabolic rate were measured with an InBody570
instrument (InBody Japan, Tokyo, Japan). The diagnosis of
type II diabetes was based on the Japanese Diabetes
Society criteria [30]. Hypertension was diagnosed if the
patient had a history of hypertension and was taking anti-
hypertensive medication or if the patient had a resting
recumbent
blood pressure of
140/90 mmHg on two
occasions.
Written informed consent was obtained from every
patient, and the study was approved by the institutional
review boards of Yotsuya Medical Cube (YMC-2009-3). A
written contract (Gun-Dai-San-2-No.348) concerning the

Liver histology
During bariatric surgery, all patients underwent a needle
liver biopsy under laparoscopic guidance with a 16G
Quick-Core biopsy needle (Cook Japan, Tokyo Japan). The
diagnosis of NASH was made histologically. For histo-
logical examinations, liver tissue specimens were ﬁxed in
10 % formalin, embedded in parafﬁn, and then stained with
hematoxylin and eosin. Two hepatologists, blinded to the
patient’s clinical condition and biochemical data, reviewed
every biopsy. NASH was histologically deﬁned as steatosis

hepatocytes with or without Mallory bodies, (3) perisinu-

Brunt’s classiﬁcation [32]. The NASH activity score was
calculated in accordance with the published criteria [32].
A follow-up liver biopsy was performed when the
patients underwent a second surgical procedure by chance
for another reason, such as gallstone removal.
Statistical analyses
All data are shown as the mean ± standard deviation. Dif-
ferences between the groups were analyzed by Fisher’s exact
probability test and Mann–Whitney U tests, when a signiﬁ-
cant difference was obtained by the Kruskal–Wallis test.
Logistic regression was used for the multivariate analysis.
Receiver operating characteristic curves were used to assess
an appropriate cutoff for the continuous variable, and the
HOMA-IR. P \ 0.05 was considered to be signiﬁcant.
Results
Patient characteristics
From October 2009 until July 2011, 113 patients under-
went bariatric surgery at our institute. After the inclusion
and exclusion criteria had been applied, there remained 102
patients who agreed to participate in this study. The 11
patients who were excluded consisted of one patient who
reported excessive alcohol consumption, two patients who
were not Japanese, two patients with severe complications,
one patient who had had a second operation, and ﬁve
patients who did not consent to participation. A liver
biopsy was performed on 102 patients during bariatric
surgery, and four patients underwent a second biopsy.
None of the patients had previously undergone a liver
biopsy, and no patients had previously received a deﬁnitive
diagnosis of NASH. The patient characteristics are shown
in Table 1. The patients included 55 males and 47 females.
The mean age was 42.7 ± 10.7 years (range 20–66 years)

had diabetes mellitus and 68 of the 102 patients (66.7 %)
also had hypertension.
Liver histology
Eighty-four of the 102 patients (82.4 %) had NAFLD, 79 had
NASH, and ﬁve had nonalcoholic fatty liver (Fig. 1). As a
result, the prevalence of NASH in the morbidly obese
Japanese patients was 77.5 % (79 of 102 patients). Accord-
ing to Brunt’s classiﬁcation, of the 79 patients with NASH,
one patient had grade 0 steatosis, 35 patients had grade 1
steatosis, 32 patients had grade 2 steatosis, and 11 patients
had grade 3 steatosis, and 25 patients had stage 1 ﬁbrosis, 38
patients had stage 2 ﬁbrosis, and 16 patients had stage 3
ﬁbrosis. No patients with liver cirrhosis were observed in this
study. The mean NASH activity score was 5.4 ± 1.4.
Four patients had a follow-up liver biopsy when they
underwent surgery for gallstones or an abdominal inci-
sional hernia. The mean NASH activity score improved to
1.8 ± 1.0 from 5.3 ± 1.3 at the ﬁrst liver biopsy. Repre-
sentative cases are shown in Fig. 2. The extent of steatosis
and that of inﬁltration of inﬂammatory cells were markedly
improved beginning 1 year after bariatric surgery. Case 1
was a 32-year-old women with a BMI of 37.2 kg/m2, who
also had prediabetes. Case 2 was a 47-year-old man with a
BMI of 58.4 kg/m2, who also had hypertension. Case 3 was
a 62-year-old man with a BMI of 45.8 kg/m2, who also had
type II diabetes mellitus and hypertension. Case 4 was a
41-year-old women with a BMI of 40.7 kg/m2, who also
had type II diabetes mellitus and hypertension.

ALT, fasting plasma glucose, and HOMA-IR levels were
independent factors associated with NASH (Table 3).
Discussion
The prevalence of NASH was 77.5 % in this prospective
Japanese cohort of patients at the time of bariatric surgery.
The risk factors independently associated with the devel-
opment of NASH were the waist-hip ratio and the ALT,
fasting plasma glucose, and HOMA-IR levels. Table 4
shows the results from previous reports from various
countries. The frequency of NASH ranged from 2.6 to

We previously showed that NAFLD was more prominent
in Japanese patients in comparison with Caucasian patients
with a similar BMI [28]. The 2005 clinical practice
guidelines for the surgical management of obesity from the
American College of Physicians state that the indication for
bariatric surgery is a BMI of 40 kg/m2 or greater, a failure
to respond to nonsurgical treatment, and complications
related to obesity [33]. Because Asians are reported to
develop obesity-related complications at a lower BMI in
comparison with Caucasians, the Asia–Paciﬁc Bariatric
Surgery Group consensus meeting recommended bariatric
surgery in Asian patients with a BMI greater than 37 kg/m2
or greater than 32 kg/m2 with diabetes or two other obe-
sity-related comorbidities [29]. This difference in the
indications for bariatric surgery from the Asia–Paciﬁc
Metabolic and Bariatric Surgery Society seems to be rea-
sonable. Our study showed that the prevalence of NASH in
this Japanese cohort of patients at the time of bariatric
surgery was higher than that of Caucasian patients. As a
result, Japanese patients with severe obesity must reduce
their body weight to a greater degree in comparison with
Caucasian patients with the same BMI in order to decrease
the risk of obesity-related complications [28].

as a predictive factor for NASH [12–14]. In this study, the
prevalence of diabetes mellitus was not a predictive factor
for NASH. However, this study revealed that the insulin
resistance factors, including the fasting plasma glucose,
fasting blood insulin, C peptide, hemoglobin A1c, and
HOMA-IR levels, were signiﬁcantly worse in the NASH
group. Furthermore, fasting plasma glucose and HOMA-IR
levels were found to be independent predictors of NASH in
a multivariate analysis. Hypertension was also found to be
signiﬁcantly associated with NASH in a previous study [6].
However, in our present study, the prevalence of hyper-
tension was not signiﬁcantly different between the NASH
and non-NASH groups. Because the number of patients in
the non-NASH group was small in this study, the preva-
lence of diabetes mellitus or hypertension was not a pre-
dictive factor for NASH. As expected, abnormal liver
function test results were signiﬁcantly related to NASH in
this study, as has been reported previously [13, 16, 18].
There has been intense interest in the development of
biochemical markers and scoring systems for predicting
NASH and ﬁbrosis [34]. To predict NASH, scoring sys-
tems including the hypertension, ALT, and insulin resis-
tance (HAIR) score [6], Palekar’s score [35], the Nash
test [36], Gholam’s score [37], the NASH clinical scoring
system [38], the Nice model [39], and the NAFIC score
[40] have been reported. Only the HAIR score and
Gholam’s score could be calculated with the factors that
were checked in the present study because we did not
measure speciﬁc factors such as cytokeratin 18, type IV
collagen 7S, hyaluronic acid, and haptoglobin. The mean
HAIR score (2.30 ± 0.74) of the NASH group was sig-
niﬁcantly higher than that (1.87 ± 0.69) of the non-
NASH group (P \ 0.05). When the cutoff index of the
HAIR score was set at 2, the sensitivity and the speciﬁcity
of the HAIR score were 83.5 and 34.8 %, respectively,
and the accuracy was 72.5 %. The sensitivity was the
same as or slightly better than that previously reported
[6]. However, the present study showed a lower level of
speciﬁcity. The mean Gholam’s score of the NASH group
(10.7 ± 1.7) was signiﬁcantly higher than that of the non-
NASH group (9.1 ± 1.4) (P \ 0.01). When the cutoff
index of Gholam’s score was set at 8.22, the sensitivity
and the speciﬁcity of Gholam’s score were 96.2 and
30.4 %, respectively. The sensitivity was better than that
previously reported (76 %) [37]. However, the present
study showed a lower level of speciﬁcity than the previ-
ous report (66 %). The accuracy of the present study was
81.3 %, which was superior to that of the previous report
(70 %). Because both the HAIR score and Gholam’s
score were derived from the data of morbidly obese
patients, our results were similar to these predictive
scores. However, the speciﬁcity of our results was worse
than that in previous reports [6, 37]. This discrepancy
may have resulted from the higher proportion of NASH
patients in the present study.
In this study, four patients had a follow-up liver biopsy,
and the ﬁndings showed there was abatement of the NASH.
Some studies have suggested that gastric bypass or rapid
weight loss may increase inﬂammation and the risk of
NASH [41], whereas Dixon et al. [42] showed that hepatic
lesions, including ﬁbrosis, were improved signiﬁcantly
after bariatric surgery and major weight loss. Because only
four patients who underwent a second biopsy were inclu-
ded in this study, further follow-up of the patients will be
needed. However, our results support the results reported
by Dixon et al. [42].
In conclusion, the prevalence of NASH was 77.5 % in
this prospective Japanese cohort of patients at the time of
bariatric surgery. The major risk factor for developing
NASH was insulin resistance in morbidly obese Japanese
patients. Early intervention will be needed for morbidly
obese Japanese patients in order to reduce the risk of
obesity-related complications.
